entries.title: BABA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Patient-Advocacy Agents
entries.abstract: An LLM agent that helps a patient get care must do two things. It must reach the correct outcome, and it must follow the necessary procedure. For example, the agent must get the patient's permission before it shares the patient's records. We introduce BABA-Bench, a benchmark of 47 interactive worlds. We built each world from a de-identified, real patient advocacy case that expert advocates reviewed. In each world, the agent must find hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, suppliers, pharmacies, and community organizations. The engine checks each action at the time the agent does it. It checks if the agent has permission, if the agent has evidence for the action, and if the action is prohibited. We evaluated 14 frontier models with three runs on each world, for a total of 1,974 runs. Agents often reached the correct outcome by an invalid route. Of the 921 runs that reached all required outcomes, 254 (28%) did not follow the necessary procedure. Claude Opus 5 reached all required outcomes in 81.6% of its runs, but only 52.5% of its runs passed all checks. When we gave two models a verified route, their pass rates increased from 29.8% to 91.5% and from 44.0% to 97.2%. For these models, the main problem is to find a route, not to execute it.

entries.title: Do Language Models Know What Compelling Scientific Evidence Looks Like?
entries.abstract: Expert scientists excel at weighing empirical findings from multiple sources that vary in both statistical reliability and epistemic relevance. To what extent are language models, which are increasingly driving autonomous discovery systems, capable of such evidence deliberation? We introduce EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark curated from real-world data in three biological domains: drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Each of EDB-Bio's 96k episodes presents a sequence of experimental results from published studies and asks the model to predict the probability that a target hypothesis is true. Out-of-the-box, open-weight and frontier models alike demonstrate systematic underconfidence and attain Brier scores comparable to a trivial base-rate forecaster. Post-training against strictly proper scoring rules significantly improves both calibration and discrimination. This calibration pays off downstream: in a sequential experiment selection task, our Ibis0 model is 2.5 times more efficient than the best frontier model. Throughout, quantifying evidence weights as Bayes factors reveals how models update their beliefs over time, whether they agree with expert biologists on relevance, and where they exhibit inconsistencies and biases. Our work extends calibration training and uncertainty analysis to a realistic scientific forecasting setting with applications to human cancer biology. We release all code, data, and trained models.

entries.title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
entries.abstract: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.

entries.title: Using iterative agentic retrieval-augmented generation to refine the risk of infection from social contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic: Development and Evaluation Study
entries.abstract:
BackgroundContact tracing is crucial to limit pathogen transmission and to gather epidemiological data. However, despite machine learning optimizations, it remains time-consuming. Large language models have been used for infection risk prediction, but no existing application converses with a user to adapt its risk estimates.

ObjectiveWe aimed to develop an iterative retrieval-augmented generation conversational framework to predict coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection risk from textual social data. The conversational agent aims to gather personalized risk factors based on descriptions of social interactions.

MethodsWe trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict the risk of COVID-19 infection from 19,434 textual descriptions of social interactions, collected during the pandemic in the Leuven student community, in Belgium. We integrated this model into a Llama3.3-based conversational framework that iteratively gathers additional social information that may represent a risk of infection. We evaluated the framework using large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics and by comparing its risk assessment in different social contexts.

ResultsBased solely on social interaction data, a fine-tuned RobBERT model predicted infection risk with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.73. It performed similarly to an LSTM model and a logistic regression on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, which both achieved a ROC AUC of 0.72. These three models slightly outperformed a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-fine-tuned Mistral NeMo model (ROC AUC = 0.69). Llama3.3 performed well in our framework: the predicted infection risk converged often, and it asked fewer redundant questions than the smaller models (Mistral 7B, Gemma3 12B). In addition, the framework showed the ability to stratify, by risk of infection, synthetic users who had different types of social interactions.

ConclusionsCombining simple language models with large language models can refine individual infection risk from contact tracing data in a high-circulation context. Our conversational framework may help optimize contact tracing by highlighting social contexts with a high risk of infection.

entries.title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
entries.abstract: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

entries.title: DiaBench: A Benchmarking Framework to Evaluate the Performance of LLMs in T2D Patient Education
entries.abstract:
BackgroundEffective type 2 diabetes (T2D) education improves patient outcomes, but clinician time constraints limit what can be covered during encounters. Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable way to answer patient questions, yet their accuracy and reliability in T2D education across health literacy levels remain poorly characterized.

MethodsWe developed DiaBench, a standardized benchmarking framework built from 96 question- and-answer pairs collected by clinicians from representative real-world patient encounters. GPT-5 transformed each pair into multiple-choice questions (MCQs) under three configurations (1-3) simulating different question formats and levels of user background. A five-member panel of certified diabetes care and education specialists (CDCESs), medical doctors (MDs), and endocrinologists validated the transformations, rating question rephrasing, answer rephrasing, and answer correctness. We then evaluated seven LLMs (GPT-51, Gemini-2.5-Flash2, Cohere Command3, Llama-44, DeepSeek-R15, Perplexity Sonar6, Mistral-Large-2.07) for accuracy and self-consistency across three runs.

Results(i) Expert validation showed a consensus over MCQ transformation. For configuration 1, 98.1% (SD 0.01) of rephrased answers were appropriate, 98.1% (SD 0.01) of MCQ answers were correct, and 95.0% (SD 0.05) of rephrased questions were appropriate; corresponding values for configuration 2 were 96.3% (SD 0.05), 97.5% (SD 0.02), and 89.8% (SD 0.14). (ii) across benchmarking for configurations 1 and 2, most models achieved high accuracy ([≥]95%), but Mistral-Large-2.0, Llama 4, and Perplexity Sonar showed substantially lower self-consistency (60.4%-91.7%) than other models ([≥]95%). All models degraded in both accuracy and self-consistency on configuration 3.

ConclusionsDiaBench quantitatively differentiates LLM capability in T2D patient education, with Gemini, GPT-5, and DeepSeek-R1 performing strongly and other models suboptimally. DiaBench provides a transferable platform for evaluating existing and newly developed LLMs, addressing the need for standardized benchmarking before clinical deployment of LLM-based systems in patient education.

entries.title: Measuring Data Leakage in the Absence of Patient Identifiers: A Public Kidney CT Benchmark and a Transferable Screen.
entries.abstract: Data leakage between training and test partitions inflates measured performance independently of a model's ability to generalise. In medical imaging its commonest form is images of one patient or acquisition in both partitions. Detecting it requires knowing which images share an origin, the field public datasets strip before release. This study measures leakage where that field is absent, in a widely used public kidney computed tomography (CT) dataset. The aim is not to restore patient identity but to recover enough of the grouping to split above the image level, and to measure what its absence has cost. A 64-bit perceptual hash read along the distributed file order resolved the 12,446 images into 219 recovered groups. These are units at the level of the acquisition, not the patient; the number of patients and their spread across groups and classes stays out of reach. Against a dataset carrying identifiers the rule divided single patients across groups more often than it merged them, so every difference reported is a lower bound. In a matched design that requires no patient identity, each of three models, trained once, scored 8.18 to 12.01 accuracy points lower on unseen groups than on seen ones, every cluster-bootstrap interval excluding zero. A nearest-neighbour rule with no learned parameters classified every test image correctly under random splitting. Of 59 studies using the dataset, two state the level at which they split. A duplicate screen applied to six further public releases returned verified overlap in three. The recovered image-to-group assignment is released.
